quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what a fixed asset is, what goes into its cost and the vocabulary of depreciation.

questions.q: A fixed asset is one that is…
options: Bought for resale within the year
Capable of repeated use with an expected life of more than one year
Always kept at its original cost
Paid for in cash rather than on credit
questions.explain: The defining features are repeated use and a life beyond one year. How it was paid for is irrelevant, and its book value falls through depreciation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the initial cost of an imported machine?
options: A routine repair after a year of use
questions.explain: Initial cost includes every expenditure needed to get the asset in place and ready for use. A routine repair after use is an expense of that period.

questions.q: The cost of land includes…
options: The negotiated price plus broker’s commission, registration and surveying fees
The price less any resale value
questions.explain: Commission, registration and surveying are needed to acquire the land, so they are capitalised. Land is not depreciated at all.

questions.q: Land is depreciated like any other fixed asset.
questions.explain: All fixed assets except land lose their capacity to yield services with time. Land is the one exception and is carried at cost.

questions.q: When a machine is removed from service and held for sale, it…
options: Continues to be depreciated as a fixed asset
Ceases to be a fixed asset
questions.explain: A fixed asset must be in repeated use; once held for sale it is no longer one.

questions.q: Depreciation is best described as…
options: Setting cash aside to replace the asset
The fall in the market value of the asset
Charging the decline in an asset’s cost to expense in a systematic manner
The cost of repairs and maintenance
questions.explain: Depreciation spreads the cost over the asset’s service life systematically. It is not a cash fund and does not track market value.

questions.q: The declining-balance method is most suitable for assets whose…
options: Productivity is the same every year
Productivity declines proportionately more in the early years
Life is less than one year
questions.explain: Heavy early charges match heavy early use, and the smaller later charges are offset by rising maintenance costs.

questions.q: Major repairs that extend the life of an asset are capitalised, that is, added to its cost.
questions.explain: Map Furniture’s Rs 13,300 of major repairs were added to the truck’s cost (137,300); the routine garage bill of 1,450 was expensed.

questions.q: The residual (trade-in) value of an asset is…
options: Its cost less the first year’s depreciation
The amount expected to be recovered when it is disposed of at the end of its useful life
The cost of the major repairs done on it
The value of the asset after installation
questions.explain: Residual value is what the asset is expected to fetch at the end of its life — 25,000 for the first truck. It is deducted from cost under straight line and is the floor under declining balance.

questions.q: The double-declining-balance rate for an asset with a five-year life is…
questions.explain: Straight-line rate = 1 ÷ 5 = 20 %; double declining uses twice that, 40 %. 50 % would be the DDB rate for a four-year life.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The three depreciation formulas, how each input moves the charge, and how book value and disposal gains are found.

questions.q: Annual straight-line depreciation equals…
questions.explain: Only the depreciable amount (cost less residual) is spread over the life: (20,000 − 2,000) ÷ 5 = 3,600. Dividing full cost by life ignores the residual.

questions.q: Under the declining-balance method the fixed rate is applied to…
options: The written-down value at the start of the year, ignoring residual value
questions.explain: The rate is applied to the written-down value (10,000, then 8,000, then 6,400…). Applying it to cost every year would give a constant charge.

questions.q: What is the double-declining-balance rate for an asset with a four-year useful life, in per cent?
questions.explain: Straight-line rate = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 %; doubled = 50 % — the rate used for the 570,000 truck.

questions.q: If the estimated useful life is made longer, the annual straight-line charge…
questions.explain: The same depreciable amount is divided by more years, so each year’s charge is smaller.

questions.q: If the estimated residual value is raised, what happens to the annual charge?
options: Straight-line charge falls; the declining-balance charge in year 1 is unchanged
Straight-line charge rises; declining-balance charge falls
questions.explain: Straight line deducts the residual before dividing, so a higher residual lowers the charge. Declining balance ignores the residual until the floor is reached.

questions.q: Under the declining-balance method the depreciation charge is the same every year.
questions.explain: The charge falls each year because the rate is applied to a shrinking book value: 2,000, 1,600, 1,280 and so on.

questions.q: The book value (written-down value) of an asset is…
options: Market value on the balance-sheet date
questions.explain: Book value is cost less all depreciation charged to date (497,000 − 218,680 = 278,320). It is not the market value.

questions.q: A gain on disposal arises when…
options: Proceeds are less than the book value
questions.explain: Gain or loss = proceeds − book value. Comparing proceeds with original cost ignores the depreciation already charged.

questions.q: An asset costs Rs 20,000, has a residual value of Rs 2,000 and a life of five years, depreciated straight line. What is its written-down value after three years?
questions.explain: Annual charge = 18,000 ÷ 5 = 3,600; after three years 10,800 has been charged; 20,000 − 10,800 = Rs 9,200.

questions.q: When an asset is bought part-way through the year, that year’s depreciation is…
options: Nil until the first full year
The annual charge ÷ 2 in every case
questions.explain: The first truck, bought in late February, was charged 10/12 of a year’s depreciation. Halving is only correct when the asset was owned for six months.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Depreciation charges, book values and disposal results from the lecture’s worksheets and a few mill assets of your own.

questions.q: A machine costs Rs 20,000, has a residual value of Rs 2,000 and a useful life of five years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
An asset costing Rs 10,000 is depreciated by the declining-balance method at 20 %. What is the depreciation charge in year 3?
questions.explain: Book value at start of year 3 = 10,000 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 6,400; charge = 6,400 × 20 % = Rs 1,280.

questions.q: An asset costing Rs 10,000 with a residual value of Rs 2,000 is depreciated at a double-declining rate of 40 %. Book value at the start of year 4 is Rs 2,160. What is the year 4 charge?
questions.explain: 40 % of 2,160 would be 864, but that would take the book value below the residual. The charge is limited to 2,160 − 2,000 = Rs 160.

questions.q: A used truck is bought for Rs 124,000 and major repairs of Rs 13,300 are capitalised. Life 3 years, trade-in value Rs 25,000, straight line. What is the depreciation for the first 10 months, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: Cost = 137,300; depreciable amount = 112,300; annual = 37,433; × 10/12 = Rs 31,194.

questions.q: A mill imports a stenter: invoice price Rs 1,800,000, import duty Rs 270,000, freight and insurance Rs 60,000, installation Rs 45,000, and first-year maintenance contract Rs 30,000. What cost is recorded for the fixed asset?
questions.explain: Cost = 1,800,000 + 270,000 + 60,000 + 45,000 = Rs 2,175,000. The maintenance contract is a running expense, not part of getting the asset ready for use.

questions.q: A truck costing Rs 497,000 (life 5 years, DDB rate 40 %) is bought on 10 September. What is the depreciation for the four months to 31 December, to the nearest rupee?
A truck cost Rs 497,000 and accumulated depreciation to the date of sale is Rs 218,680. It is sold for Rs 260,000. What is the loss on disposal?
The first truck (cost Rs 137,300) has accumulated depreciation of Rs 56,150 when it is traded in for an allowance of Rs 50,000. The result of the disposal is…
questions.explain: Book value = 137,300 − 56,150 = 81,150; allowance 50,000; loss = Rs 31,150. Rs 87,300 compares the allowance with cost and ignores depreciation.

questions.q: A loom costs Rs 3,000,000, has a residual value of Rs 300,000 and a life of 10 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
The same loom (cost Rs 3,000,000, life 10 years) is depreciated by the double-declining-balance method. What is the depreciation charge in year 2?

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill decisions on what to capitalise, which method to choose and how to record disposals.

questions.q: A mill buys a stenter from Germany. Besides the price it pays customs duty, sea freight, and for a concrete foundation. Which of these should be capitalised?
questions.explain: Every expenditure needed to get the asset in place and ready for use is part of its cost — duty, freight and foundations included.

questions.q: A delivery truck’s routine garage bill of Rs 1,450 should be…
options: Added to the cost of the truck
Charged as repair expense of the period
Treated as part of the residual value
questions.explain: Routine repairs keep the asset running but do not extend its life, so they are expensed. Only major repairs that extend life are capitalised.

questions.q: An old loom is overhauled at a cost of Rs 400,000, extending its working life by five years. The overhaul should be…
options: Capitalised and depreciated over the extended life
Ignored, since the loom is already depreciated
questions.explain: A major repair that extends life is added to cost, as Map Furniture did with the Rs 13,300 on its truck, and then depreciated.

questions.q: A dyeing plant’s new machine gives its highest output in the first years and will need rising maintenance later. Which method matches the pattern of benefit?
options: Charging the full cost in year 1
questions.explain: Declining balance charges most in the early years of heavy use and least later, when maintenance costs are rising — the lecture’s own justification for the method.

questions.q: When an asset is sold in the middle of the year, no depreciation is charged for that year.
questions.explain: Depreciation is recorded up to the date of disposal — Map Furniture charged 24,956 for the eight months before the trade-in on 10 September.

questions.q: A mill buys a machine on 1 January. Which method will report the lowest profit in the first year?
options: Declining balance at the straight-line rate
All three give the same profit
questions.explain: DDB has the largest first-year charge (4,000 on a 10,000 asset against 3,600 straight line with the lecture’s figures and 2,000 at the single rate), so first-year profit is lowest.

questions.q: A machine that cost Rs 800,000 has accumulated depreciation of Rs 620,000 and is sold for Rs 150,000. What is the loss on disposal?
A loom has been depreciated down to its residual value but is still in productive use. The mill should…
options: Continue charging depreciation at the same rate
Carry it at residual value with no further depreciation
Write it off to zero immediately
Revalue it upwards to market price
questions.explain: Depreciation should not take book value below the expected residual; once there, the charge stops, as in year 5 of the DDB worksheet (charge 0).

questions.q: Under declining balance the computed charge for year 4 would take the book value below the residual value. What should the costing office do?
options: Charge only the amount that brings book value down to the residual
Skip year 4 and charge double in year 5
questions.explain: The DDB worksheet limits the year 4 charge to 160 so that the book value stops at the residual of 2,000.

questions.q: A mill buys land for a new shed and pays registration fees and a broker’s commission. These fees should be…
options: Expensed in the year of purchase
Added to the cost of the land
Deducted from the price of the land
questions.explain: Registration, surveying and commission are part of the cost of land. Because land is not depreciated, they stay in the asset at cost.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions from Map Furniture’s three years of trucks, with the common slips that catch students out.

questions.q: The 2005 truck cost Rs 497,000 and is depreciated at 40 % DDB. After its first full year of life the book value is Rs 298,200. What is the charge for the next two months (September–October 2006), to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: Year-2 annual charge = 298,200 × 40 % = 119,280; × 2/12 = Rs 19,880, the figure in the lecture’s disposal schedule.

questions.q: The lecture charges 132,533 (= 497,000 × 40 % × 8/12) for January–August 2006 on the 2005 truck. Why is the rate applied to the full cost rather than to the book value at 1 January 2006?
options: Because the truck’s first year of life runs from September 2005 to August 2006, so those eight months are still year 1 of the asset
Because the residual value had not been deducted
Because it was an error in the worksheet
questions.explain: DDB is applied by asset-year, not calendar year. Year 1 of life (198,800) was split 4/12 into 2005 and 8/12 into 2006; year 2 begins only in September 2006.

questions.q: The first truck has a depreciable amount of Rs 112,300 over 3 years, straight line. What is the depreciation for the eight months from 1 January to the trade-in on 10 September 2005, to the nearest rupee?
Depreciation on the first truck was Rs 31,194 for 2004 and Rs 24,956 for 2005 up to the trade-in. What is the accumulated depreciation at the date of disposal?
A student applies the 20 % declining-balance rate to the original cost of Rs 10,000 every year. What pattern does this produce?
options: A constant charge of 2,000, the same as straight line with no residual
A charge that stops after year 1
questions.explain: Rate × cost each year gives 2,000 every year — a straight-line pattern. True declining balance applies the rate to the shrinking book value (2,000, 1,600, 1,280…).

questions.q: In the lecture’s double-declining example (cost Rs 10,000, residual Rs 2,000), total depreciation over the five years equals cost less residual, just as under straight line.
questions.explain: 4,000 + 2,400 + 1,440 + 160 + 0 = 8,000 = 10,000 − 2,000. The methods differ in timing, not in the total once the floor is reached.

questions.q: An asset costing Rs 10,000 is depreciated at 20 % declining balance with no floor. What is the total depreciation charged over five years, to the nearest rupee?
A truck bought on 28 August 2006 for Rs 570,000 has a four-year life and is depreciated DDB. The charge for 2006 is…
questions.explain: DDB rate for four years = 50 %; 570,000 × 50 % × 4/12 = Rs 95,000. Rs 47,500 uses the 25 % straight-line rate, and Rs 142,500 is a full year at 25 %.

questions.q: The 2006 truck cost Rs 570,000 and Rs 95,000 of depreciation was charged for 2006. What is its book value at 31 December 2006?
The 2005 truck (cost Rs 497,000, accumulated depreciation Rs 218,680) is sold for Rs 260,000 cash. Which entry closes the asset out correctly?
options: Debit Cash 260,000, debit Accumulated Depreciation 218,680, debit Loss on Disposal 18,320; credit Delivery Equipment 497,000
Debit Cash 260,000, debit Loss on Disposal 237,000; credit Delivery Equipment 497,000
Debit Delivery Equipment 497,000; credit Cash 260,000, credit Gain on Disposal 237,000
questions.explain: Both the cost and its accumulated depreciation must be removed; the difference between book value (278,320) and cash (260,000) is the loss of 18,320. Ignoring the accumulated depreciation overstates the loss.
